turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hey, come on in. You look worn out. What's been going on?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ugh. I feel like a wet rag. And would you look at my ankles.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yeah, I can see that. Tell me how the swelling's been.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Both of them. Two weeks now. I kept thinking I'd overdone it hauling bags at Costco, but they don't go back down.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do they ease up if you get your feet up? Any pain?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): A little, if I prop them up. No pain. They just feel tight, and my feet feel dead, both of them, worse at night.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Numbness too. Same two weeks?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. Came on with the swelling.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): What else brought you in today?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm peeing constantly. Every hour. It's driving me nuts, and I'm up twice a night.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): You still taking the amlodipine for your pressure, and the water pill?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Every morning. Amloadipine, uh, amlodipine, ten milligrams. The water pill is hydro chlorothyazide, I mean hydrochlorothiazide, twenty five milligrams.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Both of those, every day?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Every single day. I don't skip. My husband forgets his metformin like it's a sport.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. That's his, not yours. What numbers are you getting at home?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Mostly one thirty two over seventy eight. Sometimes the cuff says one thirty over eighty.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me get one in here. One fifty eight over ninety four. Pulse is seventy two.
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Figures. Always higher in this room. And those kids in the hall, I can't hear myself think.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): It gets loud out there, I know. Any chest pain?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No chest pain.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any fever or chills?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever. No chills.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): How's the stomach been? Nausea, vomiting, belly pain?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Stomach's fine. None of that.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Cough? Wheezing?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No cough. No wheeze. I have had a frog in my throat though, four or five days.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): More scratchy, or you're clearing it a lot?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Both. Umm. Annoying. Not a cold.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Headaches, or any change in your eyesight?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): No headaches. Eyes are the same.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Getting short of breath?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Breathing's fine.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the high blood pressure, that's been years, right?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Years. Whole reason I'm on the pills. This tiredness too, these past two weeks. I feel like a wet rag from the minute I get up. Sorry I'm snappy.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): You're alright. Let me look and listen. Pitting edema, both ankles, up past the sock line. Lungs are clear. Heart's regular, no murmur.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, scratch what I said about my chest. Yesterday I walked out to the mailbox and my chest got tight.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): You'd said no chest pain. Talk me through it.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): I know what I said. It was a squeeze. Lasted a minute. Went away once I stood still, so I figured I'd overdone it again and I didn't count it.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Did it go down your arm, or into your jaw?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Just the chest. Then it was gone.

[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): I think the ankle swelling is from the amlodipine. That one can pool fluid in the legs, and the peeing fits the water pill. I can't rule out your heart for that chest squeeze, so we'll take it seriously if it comes back.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Then change something. I'm not lining up more bottles.

[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll stop the amlodipine ten milligrams for your pressure and switch you to losartan, fifty milligrams by mouth once a day. Stay on the hydrochlorothiazide twenty five every morning for the pressure too.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Losartan. Fine. My sister won't quit pushing her biotin on me for her hair. I told her I'm not taking her stuff.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Leave the biotin, that's hers. Any medicine allergies?
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): No. None.
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm going to send you for a basic metabolic panel today, kidneys and potassium. Lab's downstairs before you head out.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Today. Wonderful.

[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come back in three weeks and we'll recheck the pressure and the ankles. Till then, feet up when you can, ease off the salt, and keep writing down the home numbers. If that chest tightness comes back, or you're short of breath just sitting, call us or go to the ER.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Three weeks. Yeah. I need to get out of here, I'm wiped.
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): Switch tomorrow morning, same time as the water pill. You're done with the amlodipine. Then go get that blood drawn.

spec.situation: Patient on amlodipine and a water tablet with swollen ankles and passing urine often; blood pressure read at clinic and at home with different numbers; doctor changes one medicine.

traps.happens: The patient describes things in colourful or sentence-like speech ('I've overdone it', 'I can't hear myself think', 'a frog in my throat', 'my feet feel dead', 'I feel like a wet rag').
traps.label_rule: Every symptom name is a short clinical noun phrase of 1 to 5 words ('voice fatigue', 'numbness in both feet', 'tiredness'), never a full sentence, never starting with I/we/my. Pure idioms that are not symptoms ('I can't hear myself think' said about classroom noise) are NOT symptoms. The patient's own words stay in the cited turn, not in the name.

features: denial_then_admission: the patient first denies a symptom, then later describes it. The label records the symptom as present (the later, fuller answer) and does NOT also record the earlier denial as a negative finding.

third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.

bad.reason: Throat frog/scratchy/clearing for 4-5 days stated; hoarseness not explicitly stated.
bad.text: hoarseness (category=ENT, status=present, duration=4 to 5 days, temporality=current, reported_by=patient, certainty=certain)

omissions.text: Home blood pressure readings were reported as mostly 132/78, sometimes 130/80.
Patient denied chest pain initially before later correcting herself to report a brief exertional chest tightness episode.
Patient denied nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain/belly pain.
Throat symptom details were that it felt like a 'frog in my throat' with throat clearing and scratchiness, and she did not think it was a cold.
Pitting edema extended up past the sock line, not just at the ankles.
Doctor instructed the patient to switch tomorrow morning, at the same time as the hydrochlorothiazide, and that she is done with amlodipine.

omissions.text: Amlodipine 10 mg was reported by the patient as being taken every morning/every single day prior to the switch, not just discontinued by the doctor.

Urinary frequency includes being up twice a night (nocturia) and is described as 'driving me nuts'; nocturia is recorded separately but the symptom was part of the patient history of constant urination.
The bilateral foot numbness was described by the patient as the feet feeling 'dead' and started at the same time as the swelling.
The throat symptom was further characterized as scratchy with frequent throat-clearing.
Chest tightness was initially denied and then corrected by the patient; this explicit correction/disagreement is not captured.

The exertional chest tightness was described as a 'squeeze' occurring on walking out to the mailbox yesterday, lasting a minute, and resolving with rest; the mailbox detail and squeeze quality are not recorded.
Negative finding: no chest pain was initially reported when asked.
Negative finding: no shortness of breath with current symptoms was denied, and the safety-net specifically added shortness of breath while sitting as an ER/call trigger.
Home blood pressures were said to be 'mostly' 132/78 and 'sometimes' 130/80, indicating usual range rather than isolated readings.
Follow-up plan included rechecking both blood pressure and ankle swelling in three weeks.
The doctor instructed the patient to get the blood drawn today/downstairs before leaving.
